The bagrid catfish Tachysurus vachellii displays life-history traits typical of a medium-sized benthic predator inhabiting temperate East Asian rivers. Females deposit demersal, adhesive eggs during a spawning event, and each newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at a minute size, with an estimated wet weight at birth of only 0.0041 grams [Wwb = 0.0041 grams]. This value was derived from the relationship between egg diameter and volume, assuming a spherical egg of 1.98 mm. The initial mass is comparable to that reported for other bagrid species, reflecting the relatively small, energy-dense oocytes characteristic of the family. The larval period is marked by progressive yolk absorption and rapid development of feeding structures, culminating in the onset of exogenous feeding approximately five to seven days after eclosion. Growth during the first growing season is substantial, driven by high summer water temperatures and abundant benthic invertebrate prey.

Juveniles undergo a gradual allometric shift as they transition from a planktonic existence to a benthic foraging mode, eventually settling into structured habitats among cobble and submerged vegetation. The total length at which individuals attain puberty has been established from histological analysis of gonadal tissue, with males and females maturing at approximately 15.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 15.5 centimeters]. This length corresponds to an estimated wet weight at puberty of 30.9 grams [Wwp = 30.9 grams], indicating a substantial investment in somatic growth before the onset of gametogenesis. The transition to reproductive maturity is accompanied by the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and the onset of vitellogenesis in females, mirroring patterns observed in other bagrid species such as Tachysurus fulvidraco. Available data from captive rearing studies suggest that puberty is reached during the second summer of life under natural thermal regimes.

Reproductive output in this species is closely tied to female body condition and water temperature. At a stable temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], females produce approximately 77 eggs per gram of body mass, a relative fecundity that serves as the basis for calculating maximum annual reproductive capacity. With an average spawning female attaining an ultimate wet weight of 591 grams [Wwi = 591 grams], the total annual egg output reaches approximately 45,507 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 45,507 eggs per year], reflecting the product of body mass and mass-specific fecundity. This annual fecundity is distributed across a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year], yielding a per-event clutch of approximately 45,507 eggs [N_R_i = clutch of approximately 45,507 eggs]. Egg diameter averages 1.98 mm, producing the small neonatal mass observed, and the adhesive, demersal eggs are deposited among cobble substrates.

Longevity data from both wild populations and captive maintenance indicate that this species has a moderate lifespan relative to its body size. At a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days]. This duration, equivalent to roughly eight years, allows individuals to participate in multiple reproductive seasons, consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy. Senescence in older adults is marked by a gradual decline in growth rate and reproductive output, with females showing reduced fecundity in later spawning events. The ultimate total length attained by the largest individuals in a population reaches 42.3 centimeters [Li = 42.3 centimeters], a size that is rarely achieved under natural conditions. This asymptotic body length is consistent with the allometric scaling relationship observed across the genus.

The ecological role of this species as a benthic invertivore influences its life-history tempo. The moderate lifespan of roughly eight years under optimal thermal conditions facilitates the accumulation of biomass across multiple growing seasons, while the relatively late onset of maturity at 15.5 centimeters length balances the trade-off between survival and early reproduction. Comparative data from congeneric species indicate that the asymptotic adult body mass of 591 grams [Wwi = 591 grams] places Tachysurus vachellii near the upper end for the genus, likely reflecting productive riverine habitats rich in benthic macroinvertebrates. The combination of a moderate body size of 42.3 centimeters [Li = 42.3 centimeters], iteroparous reproduction, and a relatively protracted juvenile period positions this species as a typical K-selected strategist within its freshwater ecosystem. Future studies examining growth trajectories under varying temperature regimes would further clarify the metabolic constraints shaping these life-history parameters.
